title: Which Lₚ-spherical copulas maximise a generalised Gini mean difference?
shortTitle: The Lₚ-spherical copula conjecture fails off unit power
oneLine: The Bernard–Müller–Oesting conjecture fails at every power except one: the conjectured optimal copulas come within parts per million of the optimum, but are never exactly optimal.
abstract: When two quantities are forecast together, fixing each one's distribution still leaves open how they move together. The energy score for multivariate forecasts and the energy distance between distributions rest on the expected distance between two independent draws, raised to a power β between 0 and 2; with both marginals uniform and only the dependence free, its maximum is a dependence uncertainty bound. At β = 1 Bernard and Müller proved that the maximiser is the disc copula, the shadow on a plane of the uniform distribution on a sphere. For other powers Bernard, Müller and Oesting introduced the Lₚ-spherical copulas and conjectured from computations that the member with p = 3 − β is optimal. This candidate proves that the conjecture fails for every β ≠ 1, and that no member of the family, for any p from 1 to ∞, is optimal except the disc copula at β = 1. Even with the best member chosen for each β, the shortfall from the optimum is bounded above and below by constant multiples of β(2 − β)(β − 1)²; the constants are not computed. The main tool is a local regularity principle: wherever an optimal law has density bounded below, its mixed derivative is smooth, and the conjectured densities have a kink on the coordinate axes. An exact rational certificate gives a concrete better copula at β = 3/2. A floating-point profile on discretised copulas suggests the shortfall is tiny: an explicit copula beats the conjectured member by between about 2 × 10⁻⁷ and 3 × 10⁻⁵ of the optimal value, so the family remains an excellent approximation. Limits: the true optimal copula for β ≠ 1 is unknown; the numerical sizes are not certified bounds; only two dimensions are treated. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1 (proof): for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞ and 0 < β < 2, the centred Lₚ-spherical copula μₚ maximises the generalised Gini mean difference over copulas only when p = 2 and β = 1. In particular Conjecture 9 of Bernard, Müller and Oesting (p = 3 − β) fails for every β ≠ 1: a smooth marginal-preserving perturbation near the axis point (0, 1/2) increases the objective.

Theorem 2 (proof): the shortfall of the best family member satisfies c β(2 − β)(β − 1)² ≤ M_β − S_β ≤ C β(2 − β)(β − 1)², with positive finite limits at both ends; the constants c and C are not computed.

Lemma 3 and Theorem 4 (proof): on any open set where an optimal law has density bounded below, its mixed derivative ∂x∂y is smooth; the conjectured densities have a kink on the coordinate axes and fail this test.

Appendix B (exact certificate): integer and rational arithmetic proves 15382/10⁹ ≤ 𝒟/4^(3/4) ≤ 305131/10⁹ for a four-corner contrast at β = p = 3/2, so an explicit four-rectangle perturbation gives a better copula. It certifies one perturbation, not the size of the gap.

Section 7 (floating point, not certified): at six powers β ≠ 1, an explicit checkerboard copula beats the conjectured member by between about 2 × 10⁻⁷ and 3 × 10⁻⁵ of the optimal value and the best member by about 10⁻⁷ to 5 × 10⁻⁶; the best p is about 3.03 at β = 0.25, against 2.75 conjectured.

narration:
When we forecast two things at once, such as the wind at two nearby sites, getting each forecast's range right still leaves open how the two move together. A standard way to score such forecasts, the energy score, rests on one number: how far apart two independent draws are on average, with each distance raised to a chosen power. So a natural question is how large that number can be when both individual distributions are fixed and only the way they depend on each other is free. The answer bounds how much the choice of dependence alone can move the score.

In the classical case the answer is a beautiful object. Scatter points evenly over a sphere and look at their shadow on a flat plane. That shadow, called the disc copula, is known to be the best possible. For other powers, three statisticians proposed a family of shapes that bend the disc towards a diamond or a square, and conjectured from computer experiments that one particular member of the family is always the best.

This release proves that the conjecture holds only in the classical case and fails at every other power. In fact no member of the whole family is ever optimal, apart from the disc itself. The idea of the proof is easy to state. If a dependence pattern were optimal, shifting a little probability in a plus, minus, minus, plus pattern on a tiny rectangle could not help. That forces the density to be smooth in a particular sense, and the conjectured densities have a tiny kink where they cross the axes. An exact calculation in whole-number arithmetic also builds a concrete better pattern for one particular power.

Yet the family comes very close. Computations suggest that it falls short by only a few parts per million, so it remains an excellent practical approximation.

The limits matter. The true best pattern is still unknown, the size estimates are numerical rather than certified, and only two dimensions are treated. This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review.
